title: Climate, seismic factors primed ‘unprecedented’ Nepal disaster - The Japan Times
description: Climate, seismic factors primed ‘unprecedented’ Nepal disaster  The Japan Times
publisher.title: The Japan Times
full_article:
The catastrophic mountain flooding in Nepal that killed more than 1,300 people was driven by a complex web of climate and seismic processes that made it nearly impossible to predict, according to an international team of scientists.

Rising global temperatures thawed permafrost and thinned glaciers along the Langtang Lirung peak in the Nepalese Himalayas, which, combined with lingering structural damage from a 2015 earthquake, weakened the mountain face, according to the study released by World Weather Attribution, a global consortium of climate scientists. Record late-summer heat and excessive meltwater then added immediate stress prior to the Aug. 26 collapse, the study added.

“This is an unprecedented disaster in the Himalayas,” said Walter Immerzeel, a mountain hydrologist at Utrecht University and co-author of the report, during a press briefing. “This was not a single trigger event.”

The findings highlight how human-induced global warming compounds mountain hazards into cascading catastrophes that push past vulnerable countries’ adaptation limits. With past emissions locking in decades of future thawing across the Himalayas, the disaster has intensified calls for the world’s rich countries to help frontline nations handle destruction that far exceeds their physical and financial resources.

The catastrophe began Aug. 26 when a massive collapse of rock and ice near the Nepal-China border triggered a high-speed debris flood that swept away border posts, market towns and hydropower plants along a key river corridor. Government estimates put the immediate economic damage at $2.7 billion — equivalent to 6.7% of Nepal’s gross domestic product. Physical damage accounted for $1.8 billion, with an additional $883 million in economic losses.

Nepal has already sought compensation from the United Nations Fund for responding to Loss and Damage, a nascent climate-aid system set up to help developing nations deal with the worst impacts of global warming. The study’s confirmation of human-caused warming as a factor provides crucial scientific backing that is expected to embolden Nepal’s claim, experts say.

“There is no doubt that climate change is one of the drivers, and therefore it needs to be discussed in the context of loss and damage,” said Friederike Otto, professor of climate science at Imperial College London and co-founder of World Weather Attribution. “These are the events that are clearly linked to human-induced climate change, and that clearly have unavoidable loss and damage.”

At its core, the disaster was driven by water destabilizing weakened rock from within, according to the study. Heavy snowfall in late 2025 followed by extreme summer heat sent massive volumes of meltwater deep into mountain crevices that had been fractured by the 2015 earthquake. As permafrost thawed and trapped fluid, the mountain face lost its structural integrity until a massive slab of rock and ice broke free.

The vulnerability extends far beyond Nepal. Across the Himalayas — home to the world’s largest store of frozen water outside the polar regions — the elevation at which the ground stays permanently frozen has been climbing by roughly 100 meters per decade, according to the study. Scientists warn that as thawing shifts higher into once-stable peaks, destabilized rock faces and volatile meltwater will pose an escalating threat to downstream communities.

“When warming destabilizes the roof of the world, no amount of local adaptation can fully shield vulnerable people downstream from this scale of destruction,” Otto said. “Without much faster action to transition to zero fossil fuel emissions we will inevitably see more disasters of this scale occurring in the years to come.”

Updated: 9:08 PM EDT Sep 16, 2026 Editorial Standards ⓘ By SIBI ARASU Associated Press

Human-caused global warming thinned glaciers and thawed mountain permafrost, likely helping to destabilize the Himalayan slope that collapsed last month and unleashed catastrophic flooding across Nepal, according to a report released Thursday.

The report by the World Weather Attribution cautioned that climate change was not the sole cause of the Aug. 26 disaster. A large 2015 Nepal earthquake may have weakened the rock years before the collapse, their analysis found.

“This disaster was not an extreme weather event, but the fingerprints of climate change are still clear to see in long-term changes,” said Ben Clarke, a climate researcher at Imperial College London who worked on the analysis, in a press statement.

More than 1,300 people were killed and over 5,000 remain missing after a massive section of rock and overlying glacier collapsed near Nepal’s border with China. The resulting torrent of water, ice, boulders and sediment swept through communities along the Trishuli River corridor and caused billions of dollars in damage.

Climate scientists said that across the Himalayas rising temperatures are causing glaciers to retreat and thawing permanently frozen ground that helps bind fractured mountain rock together. That means climate change can alter not only weather hazards such as heat and heavy rain, but the stability of the mountains themselves — threatening communities concentrated in narrow river valleys below.

The analysis did not determine whether the collapse would have happened without climate change, caused mainly by the release of greenhouse gases when fuels like oil, gas and coal are burned. However, researchers concluded that warming intensified several processes that made the slope less stable over decades.

'Threat is crystal clear': Over 12 trillion tons of ice from Greenland, Antarctica lost in 47 years

Global warming weakens high mountain slopes

The report found that one of the clearest changes directly linked to climate change was the rising elevation of the freezing threshold.

The report found that warming had pushed the altitude at which ground remains consistently frozen upward by roughly 100 meters (328 feet) per decade. This exposes rock at increasingly high elevations to longer periods above freezing, thawing permafrost and causing cracks within the ice, ultimately weakening the rock face under the ice.

Jakob Steiner, a geoscientist at the University of Graz who has worked in the Himalayan region since 2006 but is not an author of Thursday's report, said monitoring instruments around 5,000 meters (16,404 feet) now show that some rock and ground no longer remain frozen throughout the year.

“This means that the ground that was sitting below ice for hundreds and thousands of years is now becoming exposed,” said Steiner.

The report found that glacier retreat was another destabilizing force.

Glaciers in the region have been losing mass for decades at a rate equivalent to more than half a meter (about 1.6 feet) of thinning each year, the report found. The Langtang Lirung glacier, located in the region where the disaster occurred last month, has retreated about half a kilometer (0.3 miles) since the 1990s, exposing rock once covered by ice.

The Himalayan region contains the largest volume of snow and ice outside the polar regions. More than 63,000 glaciers in the area feed at least 10 major Asian river systems and support the food, water, energy and livelihood security of billions of people. However, various studies have found that around 78% of the glacier area, located between 4,500 and 6,000 meters (14,763 to 19,685 feet) above sea level, is highly exposed to warming. United Nations reports have found that between 2000 and 2019, glaciers lost 267 billion tons of ice per year, roughly equivalent to the mass of 46,500 Great Pyramids of Giza.

As glaciers shrink, they can remove pressure that helped support adjoining rock walls, while producing additional meltwater.

The weeks before the Aug. 26 collapse were also unusually warm. July and August 2026 were the warmest such months recorded locally, according to the analysis.

“Other than the potential geological factors like earthquakes that are weakening the bedrock, all these other factors are made worse by human-induced climate change,” said Friederike Otto, climate scientist at Imperial College London and one of the report's authors.

Disaster exposes limits of adaptation

The report said the catastrophe also demonstrates how some climate-related risks in the world’s highest mountains may exceed the protection that early warning systems and other adaptation measures can provide.

Nepal has developed disaster risk reduction plans and warning systems, but researchers said the size and speed of the collapse overwhelmed those defenses. Unlike a flood caused by rainfall, which can sometimes be forecast hours or days ahead, catastrophic slope failures in remote high mountains can occur suddenly and remain extremely difficult to predict.

Otto, the climate scientist, said that the mountain ecosystem and societies are more vulnerable to climate impacts than those living in the plains. “Small changes in temperatures affect the stability of the land itself,” she said.

Better high-altitude monitoring, earth observation and warning systems could reduce some risks, the report said. But researchers warned there are limits to adaptation in Himalayan valleys where settlements, roads, hydropower projects and other infrastructure are concentrated along rivers.

Since glaciers and permafrost respond to temperature changes over decades, some mountain destabilization caused by warming has already been set in motion, said the report.

“The most important thing to minimize the risk in this region is to rapidly stop using fossil fuels that lead to increasing global temperatures," said Otto. “All these drivers that we’ve talked about, permafrost melting, glacial melting, etc., will just become worse. And that means that events like this become more frequent.”

title: Opinion | How Nepal can reshape global response to climate catastrophes - The Kathmandu Post
description: Opinion | How Nepal can reshape global response to climate catastrophes  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Following the devastating floods last month that tore through settlements across several districts, the wave of support from global leaders and citizens has been extraordinary. It reflects the standing Nepal has built over decades: in UN peacekeeping, in intergovernmental forums, and most recently through a political renewal the rest of the world watched with real interest. The sympathy and support for Nepal arrived quickly because Nepal had credibility to draw on.

As Nepal confronts the challenges of rescue, resilient recovery and reconstruction, it possesses a unique blend of moral authority and political visibility. Could Nepal turn this moment into a global movement—rallying the world behind solutions that match the brutal scale of climate catastrophes?

Nepal’s experience places it at the forefront of a larger global reality. As underscored by UNEP’s September 2026 Limiting Overshoot report, exceeding the 1.5 degrees Celsius threshold is now an unavoidable reality. Yet this is not an abstract threshold for countries hit by extreme climate catastrophes. Heatwaves, floods, wildfires, droughts and glacial outbursts are striking with unprecedented intensity.

A challenge facing Nepal and the developing world is the fragmentation across humanitarian, development and climate action systems, although they address the same risks. Headline catastrophes attract brief spikes of attention. Disaster preparedness is often underfunded, despite the proven value in minimising losses and emergency response costs. Frontline communities are left exposed before disasters, overwhelmed during them, and underserved afterward. The frequency and devastation from climate catastrophes call for breaking these silos—before, during, and after crises.

This structural flaw is compounded by the limits of the climate justice architecture. While the moral argument for climate justice centres on compensation for loss and damage, the legal framework under the UNFCCC climate convention carefully avoids state liability. Mechanisms like the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) represent vital political progress, but operational gridlock and limited funding restrict actual relief.

Nepal has long championed mountain ecosystems and the cryosphere in global forums. Yet advocacy and evidence do not produce systemic change. History shows that the most significant international breakthroughs occur when vulnerable nations move from describing problems to proposing concrete solutions and building political coalitions around them. Prime Minister Mottley of Barbados led the Bridgetown Initiative, transforming climate vulnerability and debt distress into “debt pause clauses” in World Bank lending and other multilateral development bank reforms. Similarly, the Pacific Island nations designed their own mechanism called the Pacific Resilience Facility, targeting$500 million for community-level resilience.

Could Nepal propose something the world can unite around?

The systems designed around conventional climate finance cannot deliver the speed and timeliness required by climate catastrophes that undermine both mitigation and adaptation efforts.

As climate catastrophes become the norm, Nepal should propose a rapid-response feature into existing financing mechanisms, one that aligns with the full cycle of crisis preparedness, response, and recovery. Where these funds are fragmented and overlapping, a rapid response track would help reinforce coherence and synergy across these mechanisms, reducing duplication and delay.

Alongside it, as with the priority country groups in the climate funds, Nepal should advocate for a dedicated category for mountain and high-altitude countries, given the extreme vulnerability of these ecosystems and the cascading effects of cryosphere change on other ecosystems—downstream rivers, forests, agriculture, wetlands and coastal systems. To put it simply, climate catastrophes are now undermining essential investments in energy, food and agriculture, water and sanitation systems among other priority areas on climate action.

A layered disaster financing approach offers useful lessons. When Hurricane Melissa struck Jamaica in 2025, it activated a pre-arranged risk layering system—combining contingent credit, parametric insurance and catastrophe bonds—which unlocked $241 million within days: $91.9 million from the Caribbean Catastrophe Risk Insurance Facility, and a full $150 million payout on a World Bank-issued catastrophe bond.

The lesson is clear: financing needs to be ready before disaster strikes, released quickly when it does, and complemented by larger pools of finance for recovery and reconstruction.

Nationally, the response from Nepalis has shown extraordinary resolve, with citizens, the diaspora and government mobilising rapidly for the Prime Minister’s Disaster Fund. Nepal must reinforce its initial response with a compelling pitch for resilient recovery and reconstruction, anchored in an approach that ‘builds for the future’—not simply rebuilding the past, as it also strengthens internal systems to channel financing efficiently and effectively. While raising the money is challenging, the timely absorption, expenditure and reporting are just as difficult. Nepal’s case internationally will rest substantially on that record.

Nepal will have to cast a wide net to mobilise multilateral and bilateral finance, climate funds, private capital and innovative instruments, including those to buffer risks. It should bring the world's best expertise to climate-resilient infrastructure, early-warning systems, river-basin management and community resilience. And it should use reconstruction to demonstrate what multi-hazard resilience can look like in practice as a model for others. This will not be the last catastrophe of its kind.

Turning national tragedy into global reform requires a multi-track diplomacy. The coming months present a sequence of opportunities across the UN General Assembly in New York, COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, and beyond.

While the UNGA provides high-level visibility, the real diplomatic work happens outside the main hall through leaders’ dialogues, bilaterals, and media outreach—much as Pakistan demonstrated post-2022 floods to catalyse momentum on ‘loss and damage’. The UN Climate Summit is an important opportunity to address peers and lay the ground before COP31. Upcoming formal COP31 negotiations are important, but progress moves slowly in this political economy. Nepal must also look beyond to secure support from geopolitical anchors to champion our initiatives. Overall, building support across multiple constituencies and sustaining it long after the news headlines have moved is a challenge.

This is where Nepal’s political renewal matters. A country that has demonstrated its capacity to challenge an entrenched political system can bring that same spirit to the international system.

Across the globe, climate catastrophes are outpacing every model, hitting communities hardest. What they share is not geography but a system that foresees the risks but cannot move fast enough to meet them. The surge that came down the Trishuli took minutes. The rebuilding will take years.

title: Climate crisis likely behind devastating Nepal-Tibet floods that killed more than 1,300, first study finds - The Guardian
description: Climate crisis likely behind devastating Nepal-Tibet floods that killed more than 1,300, first study finds  The Guardian
publisher.title: The Guardian
full_article:
Climate breakdown probably weakened the glacier that collapsed causing catastrophic floods and killing hundreds of people in Nepal and Tibet last month, the first scientific study of the disaster has found.

Researchers identified unusually warm conditions before the glacier’s collapse, which sent an avalanche of 110m cubic metres (3,885 cu ft) of snow and ice into the valley below. This triggered flash floods on an almost unprecedented scale, hitting communities downstream without warning.

How the deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – a visual guide Read more

“Communities in Nepal are paying with their lives for a crisis driven by fossil fuel emissions thousands of miles away,” said Dr Friederike Otto, a climate science professor at Imperial College London, which carried out the study.

“When warming destabilises the roof of the world, no amount of local adaptation can fully shield vulnerable people downstream from this scale of destruction. Without much faster action to transition to zero fossil fuel emissions we will inevitably see more disasters of this scale occurring in the years to come.”

View image in fullscreen A impromptu memorial in Kathmandu commemorates some of the people killed in the flooding. Photograph: Narendra Shrestha/EPA

More than 1,300 people were killed and more than 5,000 people remain missing after a massive section of overhanging glacier and rock measuring roughly 200,000 sq metres (2,153,000 sq ft) fell from Langtang Lirung mountain on 26 August.

It dropped about 1,400 metres (4,660ft), slamming into the valley floor with such intensity that it registered as an earthquake, liquidising ice and sparking a freezing flood that careened downriver at speeds exceeding 110 mph.

The devastating flood of water, ice, rock and sediment swept away families, homes, settlements, roads, bridges and other infrastructure, leaving survivors stranded and cut off.

“Rock avalanches of this size are rare, with annual frequency estimates of approximately one event this size every 1,000–10,000 years,” the study said. “This event shows that limits to adaptation are already being reached.”

The research was unlike previous studies by Otto and her team at World Weather Attribution (WWA) – a collaborative project between Imperial and other climate specialists worldwide – in that the role of climate breakdown could not be ascribed to one particular weather event.

Instead, the researchers found the disaster was the result of a compound crisis, with a number of factors made worse by decades of atmospheric heating as a result of greenhouse gas pollution.

Dr Ben Clarke, who researches extreme weather and climate change at Imperial, said the “fingerprints of climate change” were clear in the long-term changes that happened around the glacier before its catastrophic collapse.

View image in fullscreen ‘Communities in Nepal are paying with their lives for a crisis driven by fossil fuel emissions thousands of miles away,’ said Dr Friederike Otto. Photograph: Suryams Upreti/AAP

Among the study’s key findings were:

In the region where the collapse happened, climate breakdown has caused about 2C of warming since pre-industrial times, and about 1.5C of warming in July and August specifically;

July and August 2026 were the warmest on record locally, reaching 5C above the 30-year average in the days before the collapse;

The freezing threshold in the Himalayas has risen by about 100 metres per decade since the 1980s, with higher and longer thaw temperatures weakening mountain slopes shaped by permafrost;

The warming temperature had already driven substantial glacier recession, removing stabilising ice from around the site where the collapse occurred and contributing meltwater;

A 7.8 magnitude earthquake in 2015 further contributed to slope failure, though its specific contribution to the disaster in August could not be confirmed.

Otto, Clarke and the WWA team said their study did not directly ascribe climate breakdown as the fundamental cause of the catastrophe. Instead, it was best understood as a destabilising factor on the existing geology.

Clarke said: “We found that climate change is transforming the high mountain environment, influencing many of the possible drivers of this collapse.”

View image in fullscreen A major earthquake in Nepal in 2015 may also have contributed to the glacier’s collapse. Photograph: Ishwar Rauniyar/The Guardian

Nepal has filed a formal request with the UN loss and damage fund for financial support to address the destruction caused by the flood, a process that requires proof of a link to the climate crisis. The country’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, has also demanded that top emitting nations such as China and India “wake up” and accept shared responsibility for the disaster.

Madhab Uprety, senior technical advisor for the Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre, which is part of WWA, said only aggressive cuts to global emissions could begin to address the “losses and damages faced by vulnerable frontline communities”.

He added: “In addition to the human tragedy on an unimaginable scale, the cost of recovery for this disaster is substantial. For a nation that’s done virtually nothing to contribute to this problem, it underlines the need to find fairness in helping climate vulnerable nations cope with the problems they have not unleashed.”

title: Nepal’s wetlands are under pressure. Migrator birds are losing safe havens - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal’s wetlands are under pressure. Migrator birds are losing safe havens  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Birds know no national borders. Travelling thousands of kilometres, they move across continents in search of breeding grounds, food, and warmth. If a single wetland along their arduous route dries up, becomes polluted, or falls victim to human encroachment, the consequences ripple far beyond that immediate site, impacting avian populations across another continent entirely.

Whether it is ducks gliding gracefully over water surfaces or shorebirds foraging along muddy banks, the vibrant chatter and presence of birds keep wetland ecosystems alive. Yet in recent years, these familiar sights have been quietly slipping away. Flocks that once numbered in the hundreds are dwindling at an alarming rate, and in several wetlands and lakes across Nepal, species diversity is noticeably shrinking.

Data from recent waterbird counts conducted in Nepal’s major wetlands underscores this grim reality. In 2025, surveyors recorded 96,565 aquatic birds across major sites in the country. By 2026, that number dropped to 90,688. The total number of recorded species also dwindled from 94 to 89 within the same timeframe.

The ecological shift unfolding in Nepal’s wetlands is a localised reflection of a staggering global crisis. According to the newly released State of the World’s Birds report, out of 1,843 migratory bird species evaluated worldwide, 45 percent are experiencing active population declines. Roughly one in nine—or 11 percent—of all migratory bird species are now threatened with global extinction.

Conservationists argue that the conversation must now urgently shift from merely despairing over the plight of migratory birds to examining how safe their designated sanctuaries and wetlands truly are.

Ishana Thapa, Chief Executive Officer of Bird Conservation Nepal (BCN), emphasised that safeguarding migratory birds cannot be achieved by any single nation acting in isolation.

“If a bird migrates to Nepal for the winter, protecting it while it is here is simply not enough,” said Thapa, who attended the recent Global Flyways Summit in Nairobi, Kenya. “The breeding grounds, stopover sites, and other wintering habitats that the bird relies on during the rest of the year must also be secured.”

The landmark report, presented during the summit held from September 8 to 11, paints an alarming picture of the worsening state of migratory birds worldwide.

45 percent of species declining globally

According to the report, 45 percent of the 1,843 migratory bird species surveyed globally are in decline. Meanwhile, 30 percent of species maintain stable populations, 14 percent are increasing, and the status of the remaining 11 percent remains unknown due to insufficient data.

The assessment identified 200 migratory bird species—representing 11 percent of the total—as threatened with global extinction. Among these, 32 species are critically endangered, 57 are endangered, and 111 are categorised as vulnerable. An additional 111 species have been placed in the “near threatened” category, meaning that approximately 17 percent of the world’s migratory birds are now of significant conservation concern.

The crisis is particularly acute among specific groups. Roughly 54 percent of migratory shorebird species and 49 percent of migratory seabird species are suffering population drops. Furthermore, between 47 and 51 percent of species tied to marine habitats, forests, and coastal wetlands are experiencing steady declines.

Among the four major land-based flyway systems, the East Asian-Australasian Flyway shows the highest proportion of declining species, at 53 percent. Half of the migratory bird species that utilise the world’s six marine flyways are also dwindling. Long-distance migrants traveling between Europe and Africa have seen their numbers plummet by approximately 35 percent since 1980. Quoting historical monitoring data, the report noted that in North America alone, an estimated 2.5 billion migratory birds across 419 species were lost between 1970 and 2017.

Migratory species dependent on intertidal wetlands and coastal habitats have been hit the hardest. In North America, out of 28 shorebird species monitored between 1980 and 2019, 26 showed persistent population drops, with more than half losing over 50 percent of their population. The report further noted that at least seven migratory bird species are believed to have gone completely extinct worldwide over the last 150 years.

The risk of extinction continues to escalate. A total of 102 species moved into higher risk categories due to genuine deterioration in their conservation status, while only 34 species managed to move to lower risk categories thanks to successful conservation interventions.

Human activities remain the primary cause behind these mounting threats. Severe pollution, increasing hunting, habitat fragmentation, and global temperature rises top the list of hazards.

Invasive alien species and disease currently impact 139 threatened migratory bird species, while agricultural expansion and climate change adversely affect 103 species each.

Illegal hunting and trapping threaten 99 vulnerable species, followed by pollution (96 species), urban development (71), general human disturbance (65), commercial fishing (62), energy infrastructure (55), and deforestation (39).

Illegal killing and trapping pose an ongoing menace. In Europe, the Mediterranean, the Caucasus, and the Arabian Peninsula alone, an estimated 13.1 million to 42.7 million migratory birds are illegally killed or taken from the wild every year. A vast majority of these are songbirds, captured using nets, snares, or lime sticks. On remote islands where seabirds breed, accidentally introduced invasive predators such as rodents continue to devastate nesting colonies.

The destruction and degradation of natural habitats represent another major threat. Scientific monitoring over the past decade reveals that more than half (58 percent) of the 1,099 key biodiversity areas identified as critical for migratory birds are in poor or very poor ecological condition.

In response, the report issues an urgent call for strengthened international cooperation to protect and restore critical habitats, curb illegal hunting, minimise seabird mortality from fishing gear, control invasive species, and make agriculture, forestry, and infrastructure development wildlife-friendly. Progress towards the biodiversity conservation targets adopted by 196 countries for 2030 remains dangerously slow, the document warned.

What pressure does the report place on Nepal?

Past waterbird monitoring and studies in Nepal have consistently pointed to habitat destruction, pollution, illegal hunting, human encroachment, and land-use changes as the primary threats.

Thapa noted that the global report places four key pressures on Nepal—making wetland conservation far more effective, managing entire flyway networks rather than isolated sites in isolation, integrating bird conservation into national infrastructure planning, and strengthening data sharing and long-term monitoring.

“We must focus on whether the ecological integrity of our important wetlands is being maintained, whether regular monitoring is taking place, and whether habitat degradation is being halted,” said Thapa. “Wetlands cannot be viewed as standalone locations; they must be managed as interconnected components of the broader Central Asian Flyway network.”

According to her, when decisions are made regarding the location and design of development projects—such as roads, power transmission lines, hydropower plants, irrigation schemes, urbanisation, and renewable energy infrastructure—migratory routes and critical bird habitats must be formally integrated into environmental impact assessments.

Hum Bahadur Gurung, senior Asia partnership manager at BirdLife International Asia, who also attended the Nairobi summit, emphasised the paramount importance of secure stopover sites for migratory species.

“Migratory birds do not recognise political boundaries… but during journeys spanning thousands of kilometres, they require safe places to land, feed, and rest,” said Gurung. “Ensuring the safety of these stopover sites requires robust regional cooperation among all countries along the route.”

Why are flyways crucial?

Flyways are the established geographic corridors used by bird species as they travel between their breeding grounds and non-breeding wintering areas. Globally, four main land-based flyway systems serve terrestrial and aquatic birds—the Americas Flyway, the African-Eurasian Flyway, the Central Asian Flyway, and the East Asian-Australasian Flyway.

Nepal lies within the Central Asian Flyway, which extends from Central Asia through South Asia to the Indian subcontinent. Nepal acts as a vital sanctuary along this route. Every winter, birds fleeing the freezing breeding grounds in the northern hemisphere rely on Nepal’s wetlands for shelter, food, and habitat for winter.

As they travel south, these winter visitors settle across diverse landscapes ranging from the Himalayan foothills and mid-hill valleys to the plains, lakes, and marshes of the Tarai. The majority of winter migrants are waterbirds, arriving from cold regions including Mongolia, Kyrgyzstan, Koreas, Tibet, eastern Europe, and northern India. Some species undertake staggering journeys, flying nearly 5,000 kilometres from Siberia to reach Nepal. Of the roughly 150 bird species that migrate to Nepal in winter, the vast majority are waterbirds.

If a single key wetland, forest, or coastal staging ground along this corridor is destroyed, the loss can jeopardise the entire global population of that migrating species.

Hathan Chaudhary, president of the Nepalese Ornithological Union, said migratory birds depend heavily on water bodies and agricultural fields, which must therefore be rigorously protected.

“Ducks gather in lakes and reservoirs, while Demoiselle cranes rely on open farmland. However, the excessive use of chemical pesticides in modern agriculture is causing a noticeable decline in their numbers,” said Chaudhary.

As nations across Asia push for rapid economic development, the environmental toll on wildlife continues to mount, said Gurung. “Asia is developing rapidly, and its massive energy requirements mean that birds face a growing risk of power line collisions. In wealthier nations, massive wind turbines present an additional hazard along flight paths,” said Gurung.

“If Nepal and Bhutan execute excellent conservation work but neighboring India does not, the migration corridor is effectively broken. Successful conservation is only achievable through seamless regional communication, data exchange, and cross-border collaboration,” he said.

How safe are Nepal’s wetlands?

Nepal’s wetlands serve as indispensable resting, feeding, and energy replenish hubs for migratory birds. Renowned sites such as Koshi Tappu Wildlife Reserve, Bishajari and surrounding lakes, and the wetland buffer zones of Chitwan National Park provide vital refuges for storks, herons, egrets, and cranes.

Similarly, Ghodaghodi lake in Kailali, Jagadishpur reservoir in Kapilvastu, Barju lake in Sunsari, the wetlands of Shuklaphanta and Bardiya national parks, Pokhara lakes, and in Kathmandu, the Taudaha lake and the Manohara riverbanks remain prime destinations for wintering birds.

Yet, human encroachment, pesticide contamination, and the conversion of wetlands into agricultural or commercial land are steadily shrinking these natural sanctuaries. A lack of dedicated management has caused several wetlands to dry up, and reduced water availability directly impacts bird survival.

Unplanned electricity infrastructure poses another severe collision hazard. The construction of concrete structures, hotels, and restaurants around lake perimeters directly degrades avian habitats, while noise pollution and unmanaged waste continue to drive birds away, experts say.

Chaudhary described the situation in Koshi Tappu—historically celebrated as the bird capital of Nepal—as increasingly dire. “The natural oxbow lakes and marshes here have largely dried up following historic shifts and flooding of the Koshi river,” said Chaudhary. “Where we once saw massive flocks of around 50,000 ducks, seeing even a hundred ducks today feels like a rare event.”

The aggressive spread of invasive water hyacinth in open water bodies has compounded the crisis. “In Badhaiya lake of Bardiya, invasive weeds have covered almost the entire water surface. Despite repeated cleanup efforts at Barju lake, the weed returns, preventing birds from foraging,” said Chaudhary. “Furthermore, loud picnic parties with blaring loudspeakers near wetlands disrupt the natural quiet birds require.”

In the 2026 waterbird census, half of the surveyed monitoring sites across Nepal recorded noticeable declines in species diversity compared to the previous year. Species counts dropped across Koshi Tappu Wildlife Reserve, Barju Lake, Jagadishpur reservoir, Banke National Park, Ghodaghodi lake, Nakhodi lake, Rara lake, Pokhara Valley lakes, Taudaha, and the Bagmati river corridor. While species diversity slightly rose in Chitwan and Bardiya, total bird numbers still declined.

On a positive note, both species counts and individual bird numbers showed modest gains in Dhanusha, the Kamala river, Hetauda wetlands, the Lumbini area, the Babai and Rapti rivers, Shuklaphanta, Puraini (Banke), Bannadha lake, and the Manohara floodplains.

BirdLife International recognises Koshi Tappu and Chitwan National Park as among the 32 priority sites along the Central Asian Flyway. Thapa noted that key wetlands such as Koshi Tappu, Jagadishpur reservoir, and the major river systems of Chitwan serve as crucial transit hubs for high-altitude migrants crossing the Himalayas.

Although Nepal has instituted protective legal frameworks through Ramsar site designations, protected areas, and bird sanctuaries, human pressure remains intense across most wetlands.

“Protecting the surface area of a wetland alone is not sufficient. A wetland’s true ecological viability depends on water quality, natural hydrological flow, food availability, freedom from human disturbance, control of invasive species, prevention of illegal poaching, and sustainable land-use practices in surrounding areas,” said Thapa.

Flyway conservation investment plans

Under the Nairobi Flyways Declaration, three major international development banks have pledged to formally incorporate flyway conservation into their lending frameworks. These financial institutions have committed to mobilising up to $6 billion to protect and restore critical migratory habitats along global corridors.

At the summit, the Asian Development Bank (ADB) unveiled an ambitious plan to deploy $3 billion over the next decade to safeguard at least 50 priority wetland ecosystems within the East Asian-Australasian Flyway. This investment aims to directly benefit these vital ecosystems as well as an estimated 200 million people whose livelihoods depend on them.

Similarly, the Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean announced plans to mobilise $3 billion to $5 billion by 2050 to conserve more than 30 critical landscapes and seascapes. Meanwhile, the World Bank and BirdLife International reaffirmed their commitments to direct billions of dollars towards securing flyways used by over two billion migratory birds across Africa, Europe, and Asia.

In June 2026, the Global Environment Facility approved the establishment of the Global Flyways Grant Mechanism. The facility includes $89.7 million in direct grant funding alongside $107 million in co-financing. This initiative aims to restore and protect 9 million hectares of degraded wetlands and directly benefit an estimated 330,000 local community members.

Since 2021, multilateral development banks have successfully mobilised over $6 billion in conservation-focused financing. BirdLife International highlighted these commitments as a monumental shift towards globally coordinated flyway conservation.

Birds fly thousands of exhausting kilometres to reach Nepal every year. Yet their journey does not end in these valleys and plains; the return leg across mountain ranges and deserts is equally grueling. If a single stopover wetland disappears from their path, it disrupts far more than an individual flight—it threatens an ancient migratory cycle refined over countless generations.

“Of the globally threatened bird species, 40 are found in Nepal, and their populations here have remained relatively stable so far,” said Chaudhary. “However, we cannot afford to be complacent. As conservationists, our role is to identify the problems and point out the threats. The responsibility for executing solutions lies squarely with the government. The Department of National Parks and Wildlife Conservation, the Ministry of Forests and Environment, and non-governmental organisations must build far tighter coordination to safeguard these vulnerable species.”

In Nepal, both the number of waterfowl and the number of recorded species in key wetlands decreased over the year. Counts recorded 96,565 birds of 94 species in 2025, compared with 90,688 birds of 89 species in 2026, Kathmandu Post reports.

Nepal lies on the Central Asian Flyway, along which birds travel between breeding and wintering grounds. Around 150 species, mostly waterfowl, arrive in the country each winter. Some birds travel nearly 5,000 kilometers from Siberia, and their wintering areas include the lakes, marshes and plains of the Terai.

Decline at many locations

During the 2026 count, approximately half of the monitoring sites recorded a decline in species diversity compared with the previous year. The number of species decreased, in particular, at the Koshi Tappu Wildlife Reserve, Barju Lake, Jagadishpur Reservoir, Banke National Park, near Ghodaghodi, Rara and Taudaha lakes, in the Pokhara Lake Valley and along the Bagmati River.

In Chitwan and Bardia, species diversity increased slightly, but the overall number of birds there also declined. At the same time, a moderate increase in the number of species and individuals was recorded in Dhanusha district, near the Kamala River, in the Hetauda wetlands, the Lumbini area, on the Babai and Rapti rivers, in Shuklaphanta, Puraina, near Bannadha Lake and on the Manohara floodplain.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Pressure on wetlands

Experts link risks to birds to habitat destruction and development, pollution, illegal hunting, pesticide use and changes in land use. Additional threats include the drying up of water bodies, the spread of invasive water hyacinth, noise from recreation near lakes, waste and bird collisions with power grids.

Ishana Thapa, executive director of Bird Conservation Nepal, stressed that protecting birds in Nepal alone is insufficient: breeding, stopover and wintering sites must be preserved along the entire route. She also called for migration routes and critically important bird habitats to be considered during environmental impact assessments for roads, power lines, hydropower and other infrastructure projects.

According to the State of the World’s Birds report, 45% of the 1,843 migratory bird species assessed worldwide are declining, while 200 species, or 11%, are globally threatened with extinction. Migratory shorebirds and seabirds are suffering the most, and 58% of 1,099 key biodiversity areas important for migratory birds have poor or very poor ecological conditions.

title: The lonely grind of Nepal’s para powerlifters - The Kathmandu Post
description: The lonely grind of Nepal’s para powerlifters  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Every morning, Pawan Gharti Magar and Rajani Rai travel to a gym that lies kilometres away from where they stay. Magar, who lives in Tokha, rides for around 20 kilometres to reach the Himalayan Fitness and Gym in Satdobato, Lalitpur. Rai, who lives in Jorpati, takes a 15-kilometre ride to reach the same gym.

Magar has a short stature, and Rai is a wheelchair user with an L5 spinal injury. They are the two Nepali para powerlifters who got wildcard entries to the Asian main event, taking place in Nagoya, Japan, from October 18. They will be competing in the bench press category. Training at a nearby gym would have saved them time and resources, and offer more time for recovery after demanding sessions. But the gym in Satdobato is the only one which has a specialised bench for para powerlifters.

Magar and Rai have faced a lot of hurdles already after joining para powerlifting and representing the country at the world stage. But they are still continuing despite the state continuing to neglect them. They want to show how far they can go despite zero support from the state. They say they do it for the love of the game, inspired by nothing but a desire to put Nepal on the world para powerlifting map.

Before they can contend with the plates on the bar, para powerlifters must contend with the limitations of their own bodies. Able-bodied athletes do the bench press with their legs down, supporting their lift. Para athletes, meanwhile, compete by lying on a World Para Powerlifting-approved bench. Magar and Rai arrive at the gym in turns because a single bench is not sufficient for both to come at once and practice.

But the troubles do not exist in accessibility alone. While the gym has not charged the duo for using the facility, Magar and Rai have been covering the cost of their travel, diet and necessary accessories through the money they earn by doing jobs.

Arriving at 7am on an e-bike, Magar trains up to 8:30am and leaves for Samakhusi, where he works at a manpower company, giving orientation to migrant workers.

Rai, meanwhile, reaches the gym at 9am on a modified scooter, with coach Kelvin Maharjan waiting at the gym’s doorsteps to help her enter the gym. She needs assistance to enter and exit the gym, which has a raised concrete threshold at the entrance that forces visitors to step high or hop over—an insurmountable barrier for anyone on wheels.

The troubles that Magar and Rai go through to reach the gym daily, except on weekends, are not for themselves. It is all for winning medals for the country, the athletes say.

Rai works online at CloudFactory, a software company. “I come to the gym after completing half of my work,” she said. “I return to my room and sit in front of my laptop again.”

In 2013, Rai, who was then 14, fell off a tree in her home district of Khotang and injured her spine. After receiving treatment at the Dharan-based BP Koirala Institute of Health Sciences, Rai relocated to Kathmandu, where she could get easy access to regular follow-up and continue her education.

Doing powerlifting while in a wheelchair was, meanwhile, something that Rai had never thought of.

“I used to play different sports when I was all well,” Rai said with a wide smile. “I had thought of trying some other para sports, but when I found out that I could also do powerlifting, it changed everything.”

Rai’s first international participation was the 2017 WPPO Asian Youth Para Games in Dubai. She had participated as a newbie.

“Powerlifting was completely new to me then,” Rai recalls. After training for a couple of months, she went to Dubai and took part in the Asian Para Games. “It was a great experience,” she says.

Rai credits Tek Bahadur Gurung, the president of the National Para Powerlifting Sport Association of Nepal who she refers fondly as ‘Tek guru’, for introducing her to the sport in 2017.

Rai has not stopped lifting weights since then. She has participated in three national tournaments after that, winning them all.

But these years have not been easy for her. The lack of proper funding and investment in para powerlifting has led Rai to spend out of her pocket to fight for a medal for the country. “Let’s see how long I can continue,” Rai added with a grin.

Rajani Rai after winning the Valley-wide para powerlifting championship in June. Courtesy of NPPPSAN

Magar said he also wants to test how long he can continue lifting weights as a national para powerlifting athlete.

“I think I can keep lifting weights for a long time in the future,” Magar said, flexing his biceps.

Magar clinched gold in his weight category (up to 49kg) at the valley-wide para powerlifting championship organised with the support of Kathmandu Metropolitan City in June. There he also set a new personal record, lifting 90kg.

The bench, which was donated by the World Para Powerlifting (WPPO) in collaboration with ZKC Barbell Co, for the championship was carried from the gym in Satdobato as there are no other benches for para powerlifters in the country.

“I know the gap between me and the para powerlifters around the world,” Magar said, catching his breath after an intense training session at the gym. “If I could get at least half the facilities those world-class powerlifters get, I could beat them.”

Even Magar cannot get access to the bench all the time because travelling daily to Satdobato from Tokha throughout the year does not just fit in.

“Whenever there is a tournament, I start going to Satdobato,” Magar told the Post. “On other days, I go to a gym near my room in Tokha to stay in form.”

It is not that powerlifting was the only choice for Magar. This was not the life he had asked for. Sometimes he feels that continuing wrestling would have been better too.

“A friend of mine, who is also like me, had known a director, who knew someone in Nepal’s wrestling scene—like the WWE,” Magar shared. “With two fighters of short stature, the wrestling scene believed it could entertain the crowd more. I wrestled for around two years—from 2017 to 2019—before beginning powerlifting.”

But he says he wants to be known as a para powerlifter, for which he needs to win medals internationally in the sport.

Magar was among the three para athletes who were present at the National Sports Council on August 19 with representatives of around half a dozen para sports associations, whose athletes are participating in the 5th Asian Para Games.

Para powerlifting, alongside other para sports associations, do not get any significant support from the state throughout the year. It is something they have been suffering with for a long time, but they have high hopes during the tournaments like the Asian Para Games.

The delegation had reached the NSC demanding a closed camp for the para athletes. NSC’s member secretary Ram Charitra Mehta had then asked them to come after a week, until which he would manage something for them. Around a month has passed since then, and the para athletes are still training without state support.

Magar debuted in the 2022 Asian Para Games in Hangzhou, China, in October 2023. Weighing 48.40kg, he lifted 76kg in his first attempt, but failed the second attempt—82kg—and the third—87kg. The winner in his category was Jordan’s Omar Sami Hamadeh Qarada, who lifted 173kg, 177kg and 182kg.

“We athletes give our all just to represent the country and compete with the world but what do we get in return?” questions Magar. “From what we have heard, we might have to chip in some money to be able to fly to Japan, as the government’s financial support is nowhere close to afford it.”

Rai, meanwhile, has a personal record of lifting 40kg. In her category, Cui Zhe, the winner of the 4th Asian Para Games, had lifted 116kg.

Despite how big a gap there is between Nepali and foreign para powerlifters, the weight Magar and Rai can still lift is no joke.

“It is a big achievement if you start lifting the weight as equal as your body’s weight,” Poonam Chaudhary, who was participating in the Himalayan Pro, a national powerlifting tournament for able-bodied powerlifters, in Lalitpur on Saturday, told the Post. “If Rai, with a spinal injury, can lift 40kg, it is already a big thing. It is, however, a different aspect that she can lift far more with better training, diet and other facilities.”

“Pawan and Rajani have improved over time,” Maharjan, the duo’s coach, told the Post. “Sky is the limit, but they would need more support to reach there.”

title: Booktalk: Tika Prasad Dhakal on the 1923 treaty, Nepal’s independence and the craft of diplomacy - The Kathmandu Post
description: Booktalk: Tika Prasad Dhakal on the 1923 treaty, Nepal’s independence and the craft of diplomacy  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
In 1923, Nepal and Britain signed a treaty that formally reaffirmed Britain’s recognition of Nepal as an independent and sovereign state and marked a new phase in the two countries’ diplomatic relationship. More than a century later, the treaty continues to offer a window into Nepal’s place in a changing world and the ways a small state navigated its relationship with a global power.

‘State and Craft: Readings on the 1923 Nepal-Britain Friendship Treaty’, edited by Tika Prasad Dhakal , brings together essays that examine the treaty, the diplomacy behind it, and its place in Nepal’s modern history.

Dhakal has a PhD in political science. His work focuses on theoretical frameworks, international relations, Nepal’s foreign policy, and transitional justice. He has previously served in public offices as Nepal’s presidential advisor and as a transitional justice commissioner.

In this conversation with the Post ’s Anish Ghimire , Dhakal discusses what the treaty tells us about Nepal’s diplomatic history, how its meaning has evolved over the past century, and what it can teach us about Nepal’s foreign relations today.

Let’s begin with the book itself. What prompted you to bring together ‘State and Craft: Readings on the 1923 Nepal-Britain Friendship Treaty’? Why did you feel this treaty needed to be revisited now?

When I read the historical texts of our country, and whenever there were discussions in Kathmandu about treaties, the 1923 treaty was often underdiscussed.

There are contexts that are often discussed, but this treaty, despite its importance, receives very little mention. That actually prompted me to start researching the treaty, its background, and the several characters who were associated with it. And the deeper I went into it, the more it appealed to me.

We needed to revisit the treaty at this particular moment because of its centenary. In 2023, there was a centenary conference on the treaty, organised by Madan Puraskar Pustakalaya and the Britain-Nepal Academy Council.

Because I had already been researching the treaty since 2019, I was asked to prepare a keynote for that conference. Several articles and papers were also presented, though in their raw, very early forms. That centenary conference was actually the moment when we thought it was appropriate to revisit the treaty.

The title uses the words ‘State and Craft’. What does ‘craft’ refer to here, and what does the book tell us about the craft of diplomacy at the time?

By ‘craft’, I mean the art of handling state affairs, particularly in relation to our conduct in the neighbourhood. In international relations, states are considered rational actors, but states are abstract. They need individuals to act on their behalf. So when we look at individuals—their demeanour, character and ways of presenting things—we are looking at the craft of diplomacy.

For example, when Chandra Shumsher proposed the treaty to the Prince of Wales, who later became King Edward VIII, we see a certain level of statecraft and presence of mind. Chandra Shumsher had a good command of English and was able to communicate directly. Other Nepali officials associated with the treaty, were also highly capable in language and diplomacy. Their letters and communications, including those to the League of Nations, demonstrate this.

So, ‘craft’ is not only about what the Nepali or British sides did, but how they did it—how they conducted themselves during difficult negotiations, dealt with hurdles and reached agreements. The Nepali side had to deal with powerful British officials who were opposed to the treaty, while Viceroy Lord Reading played an important role as a link between Chandra Shumsher and the British authorities.

The craft of diplomacy is therefore about the art, patience and perseverance displayed in conducting state affairs. Although these events took place about 100 years ago, they still tell us something about how diplomacy needs to be conducted today.

This brings me to my next question. The treaty we’re discussing is more than a century old now. Which parts of it continue to have relevance for Nepal’s foreign policy or its relationship with Britain today?

I think the first article is the most consequential because it explicitly recognises Nepal’s internal and external independence. This was an agreement with Britain, the only superpower and great power of the time, which had just emerged victorious from the First World War. Britain was the dominant power in the international system, so having it unequivocally recognise Nepal’s independence was significant.

The treaty also helped shape how Nepal was presented to the outside world. Through British newspapers and the British state narrative, Nepal was presented as a congenial place, and that narrative travelled across Europe and the wider Western world, generating greater interest in Nepal.

When states call a treaty a ‘friendship treaty’, what does that language do? Does it describe the relationship, or does it also help construct a particular story about the relationship?

The way the treaty was named ‘Treaty of Friendship’ is interesting. Since the Treaty of Sugauli, Nepal had considered that treaty unequal because Nepal had lost the war. And afterwards, British policy towards Nepal’s independence remained ambiguous, which the Nepali side objected to repeatedly. For example, Britain only began addressing the Nepali King as ‘His Majesty’ in 1920, placing him on an equal footing with the British monarch.

So why did we call the 1923 treaty a treaty of friendship? Chandra Shumsher was determined to end that ambiguity over Nepal’s independence once and for all. That is why he proposed the treaty to the Prince of Wales and himself called it the Treaty of Friendship. His argument was that once Britain unequivocally recognised Nepal’s internal and external independence, the two countries were dealing with each other as equals. The British press also described the 1923 treaty as an agreement between equals.

In 1953, a British journalist wrote about the Everest expedition and linked the expedition’s success and the good relationship between Nepal and Britain to the fact that the two countries had signed a treaty ‘between equals’ in 1923.

So, the term ‘friendship’ was not simply descriptive; it became part of the story both sides told about their relationship.

After spending so much time with the treaty and the history surrounding it, has your understanding of Nepal’s relationship with Britain changed?

I have come to appreciate Nepali history a little more than I used to. The Gorkha connection is certainly one of the major links between Nepal and Britain, and Britain has also stood by Nepal at some difficult and critical junctures.

For example, when Nepal’s independence was questioned in the 1950s, particularly when Nepal applied for United Nations membership, the British government supported Nepal in international forums and testified that Nepal was a free and independent country.

What does the treaty tell us about how small states like Nepal have historically navigated relationships with powerful countries and are there lessons in that for Nepal’s diplomacy today?

There are lessons, certainly. History tells us that durable partnerships and friendships are built through institutions. Foreign policy is a continuous, institutional process. It is a dedicated and disciplined defence of the national interest.

Also, instead of calling Nepal ‘small state’, I would use the word ‘non-dominant’.

For a non-dominant country like Nepal, we need to preserve our room for manoeuvre and maintain friendships. That is why we need to value the treaties we have signed in history, even when they were signed in very different contexts. Even the most complex issues with our neighbours—border management, trade, transit and water resources—demand continuous diplomatic engagement based on mutual trust.

Diplomatic noise and posturing might bring temporary applause from a domestic audience, but they are unhelpful in solving problems. We need quietness, discipline and a sober defence of our sovereign independence.

Tika Prasad Dhakal’s five book recommendations

Sophie’s World

Author: Jostein Gaarder

Year: 1991

Publisher: Aschehoug

Gaarder’s book on philosophy has left a lasting impression on me. I’ve read it three times, and I would happily read it again.

Mukam Ranamaidan

Author: Mohan Mainali

Year: 2023

Publisher: Book Hill

Mainali’s research book tells the story of the Anglo-Nepalese War, showcasing the bravery of Nepalis during the conflict.

A History of Western Philosophy

Author: Bertrand Russell

Year: 1945

Publisher: Simon & Schuster

It taught me to break the boundaries of existing ideas and go beyond them—to venture out and think differently.

Why Nations Fail

Author: Daron Acemoglu and James A Robinson

Year: 2012

Publisher: Crown Publishers

I have quite a few disagreements with the book, but I still recommend it. It shows us the kind of research perspective we should have.

Diplomacy

Author: Henry Kissinger

Year: 1994

Publisher: Simon & Schuster

Global warming likely contributed to the deadly flash flood in the Himalayas in August, according to an analysis by the research initiative World Weather Attribution (WWA) released on Thursday.

At least 1,400 people died and more than 5,000 remain missing after a large section of a mountain, including a glacier, collapsed in the border region of Nepal and China in late August.

The resulting rock-ice avalanche rapidly transformed into a debris flood and then a water-dominated flash flood that travelled downstream at average speeds of 188 kilometres per hour, the WWA said.

"No existing early warning system could have provided sufficient lead time or prevented the scale of impacts observed in the worst-affected areas, highlighting the limits of adaptation," the WWA said.

"In a rapidly warming Himalaya, increasingly extreme and complex hazards are exceeding adaptation capacity, resulting in loss and damage. This is occurring against a baseline of a high frequency of large earthquakes, which both destabilises slopes and hampers recovery from successive disasters."

title: Nepal publishes collection on 1923 treaty with Britain — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: Nepal publishes collection on 1923 treaty with Britain — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
Nepal has published the book State and Craft: Readings on the 1923 Nepal-Britain Friendship Treaty, dedicated to the friendship treaty between Nepal and Great Britain concluded in 1923. Edited by Tika Prasad Dhakal, the collection brings together essays on the document, the diplomacy surrounding it, and its place in Nepal’s modern history.

In an interview with the Kathmandu Post, Dhakal said he began researching the agreement because of insufficient attention to it in Nepalese historical works and discussions of treaties. He had been working on the subject since 2019, and a conference marking the treaty’s centenary in 2023 provided the impetus for preparing the publication. It was organized by Madan Puraskar Pustakalaya and the Britain-Nepal Academy Council.

Recognition of independence

According to Dhakal, the most significant provision is the treaty’s first article, which explicitly recognized Nepal’s internal and external independence. He emphasized that Great Britain was the dominant force in the international system after World War I, making such recognition particularly important for Nepal.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

The editor also noted that the title “friendship treaty” not only described bilateral relations but also helped shape the perception of them as relations between equal parties. After the Treaty of Sugauli, the Nepalese side considered relations with Britain unequal, while British policy toward Nepal’s independence, he said, remained ambiguous.

Diplomatic experience

Dhakal described diplomacy as the art of conducting state affairs, dependent not only on formal decisions but also on officials’ ability to communicate, negotiate, and overcome obstacles. As an example, he cited Chandra Shumsher, who proposed the treaty to the Prince of Wales, the future King Edward VIII. According to Dhakal, Lord Reading, the Viceroy of India, also played an important role in the negotiations.

In the book editor’s view, it is important for Nepal, as a “non-dominant” state, to preserve room for maneuver and maintain friendly ties. He believes that issues of border management, trade, transit, and water resources in relations with neighbors require constant diplomatic engagement and mutual trust.

title: Nepal’s para powerlifters fund their own training — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: Nepal’s para powerlifters fund their own training — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
In Lalitpur, Nepal, para powerlifters Pawan Gharti Magar and Rajani Rai are preparing for the 5th Asian Para Games in Nagoya, Japan, spending their own money on travel, food and sports equipment. Both received wild cards to compete in bench press events scheduled to begin on October 18, Kathmandu Post reports.

Magar travels about 20 kilometres every day from Tokha to the Himalayan Fitness and Gym in Satdobato. Rai, who uses a wheelchair due to an L5-level spinal injury, travels about 15 kilometres there from Jorpati. The gym has the country’s only specialized para powerlifting bench, so the athletes train in turns.

Barriers to training

The gym does not charge the athletes for use, but they cover other expenses themselves. Magar arrives on an electric bicycle at seven in the morning, trains until 8:30, and then works for an employment company, where he conducts briefings for labour migrants. Rai works online for CloudFactory and combines work with training.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Rai needs the help of coach Kelvin Maharjan to enter the gym: there is a raised concrete threshold at the entrance, which is an obstacle for a wheelchair user. According to the athletes, they continue training in pursuit of medals for Nepal despite the lack of consistent state support.

Results and need for support

In June, Magar won his under-49 kg weight category at the Kathmandu Valley para powerlifting championship and set a personal record of 90 kg. His previous international debut came at the Asian Para Games in Hangzhou in October 2023, where he lifted 76 kg. Rai’s personal record is 40 kg; she has competed in three national tournaments and won each of them.

In August, Magar, along with other para athletes and representatives of sports associations, appealed to Nepal’s National Sports Council, demanding that it organize a closed training camp. According to the publication, about a month after the meeting, the athletes were still training without state support. Magar also said that athletes would likely have to pay part of their airfare to Japan themselves.

title: Climate change likely to have helped trigger Nepal glacier collapse, scientists say - The Kathmandu Post
description: Climate change likely to have helped trigger Nepal glacier collapse, scientists say  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Climate change is highly likely to have contributed to the catastrophic glacier collapse that flooded parts of Nepal and Tibet in late August, killing around 1,400 people and ​leaving thousands still missing, scientists said on Thursday.

Rapidly warming temperatures in the region ‌have caused glaciers to thin and have melted ice and permafrost buried deep in the bedrock of the Himalayas, according to the World Weather Attribution (WWA) group of researchers.

While it is difficult to ascertain the precise ​role played by climate change in the collapse of around 2 sq km (0.8 sq ​miles) of rock wall and glacier ice on the Langtang Lirung mountain ⁠last month, soaring temperatures created the preconditions that made it more likely, researchers involved in ​the study said.

"There's absolutely no doubt that human induced climate change played a role here ​in the preconditioning of the disaster through permafrost thawing, through thinning of the glaciers, through having more rainfall instead of snow," said Friederike Otto, a climatologist at Imperial College London.

WWA uses peer-reviewed methods to assess ​the role played by global warming in extreme weather events, according to its website.

The study ​said mean temperatures were around 5 degrees Celsius (9 degrees Fahrenheit) higher than normal in the Himalayan region ‌in ⁠August, with 1.5 C of the increase coming from climate change.

Unusually high levels of snowfall in October and November of last year also added to the volume of meltwater once temperatures began to rise, which could have helped trigger the glacier collapse, according to the study.

Glaciers ​in the region have ​been thinning by about ⁠half a metre per year (about 1.6 feet) since the year 2000, changing stresses on the rock. Melting permafrost is also likely to ​have weakened the rock wall, the study said.

A 7.8 magnitude earthquake that ​hit the ⁠same mountain in 2015 could have played a role by weakening the underlying bedrock as well, but its precise impact is unclear.

title: Even gods were not spared by the flood - Nepali Times
description: Even gods were not spared by the flood  Nepali Times
publisher.title: Nepali Times
full_article:
Before any account of temples and shrines lost to the Rasuwa–Nuwakot flood can be written, we must say that far more than monuments were lost.

We lost neighbours, friends, and collaborators who had opened their homes and memories with us at the Nepal Heritage Documentation Project. Our teams worked closely with local families, priests, caretakers, and elders.

They shared historical photographs pulled from attics and family albums, pointed us to archives and unpublished manuscripts. They walked us through rituals and processions, explained the meaning of masks and images, and passed on mythological narrations that exist nowhere in writing — carried orally from one generation to the next.

Some of these people and their loved ones were taken away by the terrible flood. Their knowledge, voices, and very presence in this world are gone.

On a scientific level, the one consolation is that documentation now exists that may help support any future reconstruction of these cultural sites, even though it is far too early to speak of rebuilding.

Kulabhakteśvara Mandira at Purano Bazar

CIVILISATIONAL CORRIDOR

Rasuwa and Nuwakot sit along ancient trade routes that once linked India, Nepal, and Tibet. Its cultural fabric reflects that history: predominantly Hindu, but home to Buddhist communities, with shamanic and folk practices woven through both traditions.

The river that carried the great flood down from the mountains carried deep cultural weight of its own. Hindus cremated their dead along its banks, which is why so many temples, shrines, and gathering places cluster along the water. The very geography that made the region sacred is what made it vulnerable.

It is easy to think of heritage as something static: old stone, old wood, old paint, catalogued and admired. In Rasuwa and Nuwakot, as across much of Nepal, this could not be further from the truth. The temples that lined these valleys were not museums, they were, and are, houses of deities — dwellings where gods and goddesses are worshipped daily through offerings, lamps, songs, and processions that structure life’s rhythms.

The ghat along the rivers are where protective deities are believed to protect towns and villages around them. This is where the dead are sent onward through rites that have been performed in largely unbroken form for centuries.

To lose a ghat or a shrine in a flood is not just structural, it means losing the physical anchor of a community's relationship with its gods, its ancestors, and its dead.

This is why heritage in this part of the world, is also a method of caring for people in trauma. In the aftermath of disaster, the resumption of ritual life — lighting a lamp at the accustomed hour, carrying a deity in procession along its original route, performing the rites owed to the dead — offers a small but real measure of reassurance.

It means: ‘something of what we knew still holds’. Many death rituals central to grieving in this region are themselves tied to specific monuments, ghat and shrines. When those places are swept away, the rituals that depend on them are left without a home at precisely the moment communities need them most.

In Nepali households, private deities are venerated daily and treated almost like family members. And when the flood left bodies unrecoverable, families in the region asked whether an effigy woven from sacred grass could stand in for the missing dead at the funeral pyre, so that the departed could still be released into their next state.

Rāmacandra Mandira at Uttaragayā

It is a small ritual improvisation, but a telling one: proof that even when the physical anchors of mourning are gone, communities find ways to keep the rites moving forward. I also recall the account of a man who survived nine days trapped in a collapsed tunnel by reciting mantra without pause — a reminder of how deeply religious practice runs through the way people in this region endure catastrophe, not only mourn it.

LOST HISTORY

The Nepal Heritage Documentation Project had documented more than 80 temples, shrines, and cremation sites along the river. Of these, 21 were completely destroyed by the flood. Many more stand damaged, their foundations undercut, their courtyards buried under silt and debris.

The Rasuwa–Nuwakot documentation is part of a larger effort that followed the 2015 earthquake and backed for eight years by the UK-based Arcadia, in coordination with UNESCO. The Nepal Heritage Documentation Project run jointly by Heidelberg University, in cooperation with the Department of Archaeology and the Saraf Foundation documented more than 2,000 monuments across Nepal in response to earthquake risk, but some of them are now lost due to a flood catastrophe attributed to climate change.

In cooperation with the Department of Archaeology and the Saraf Foundation, the Nepal Heritage Documentation Project had already prepared detailed field documentation of the condition and intangible heritage of the area. It is now the only surviving record of much of what stood there.

The Nuwakot Museum has already begun planning to match recovered objects — statues, ritual items, fragments carried far from where they once stood — back to their original sites. It is delicate, deliberate work, carried out jointly with the museum and the Department of Archaeology.

It was made possible because the project's database holds not only dates and photographs but also records of the religious practices, cult groups, and living traditions tied to each site. In much the same way that recovered bodies are being matched against the missing, recovered fragments of heritage are now being matched against a record of what once stood. The two parallel efforts, are racing against loss.

When the time for rebuilding does come, this detailed documentation will be indispensable. It will help identify where each site once stood, where each deity was housed, and where other artefacts — images, ritual objects, inscriptions — that were swept away by the flood may be traced or, if recovered, correctly returned to their place and context.

Rātomatsyandranātha Mandira at Purano Bazar

What has happened in Rasuwa and Nuwakot is, among other things, a stark argument for more comprehensive heritage documentation across Nepal — not as an academic exercise, but as an act of care for future generations.

History, recorded with sufficient care and detail, serves as memory for the future's own making: for the communities who will one day rebuild, for the children who will grow up asking what once stood where, and for a country whose sense of itself is woven through with sites like these.

The flood that struck Rasuwa and Nuwakot took lives that can never be replaced, and it took places that will now exist chiefly in memory, in photographs, and in the field notes of projects like this one.

Both losses deserve to be memorialised. Both are reasons enough to keep documenting carefully, patiently, and in close partnership with the communities whose heritage it truly is.
